## 1

Ugh, months of that grinds you down in a way that's hard to explain to anyone who isn't living it. I'm really sorry — and for the record, I don't think you're overreacting.

Honest question, though: do you actually want to quit, or has your brain just latched onto quitting as the escape hatch because nothing else has worked? Either answer is okay. If it's the first one, I'm fully behind you — the only thing I'd ask is that you spend one evening on the boring logistics first: notice period, savings runway, whether anything else is lined up. That's not me talking you out of it. It's making sure you're leaving on your terms rather than just bolting, because that version of quitting tends to feel good for longer than a week.

But if you just need out, you need out, and I'm not going to argue with you about it. Do you want to call tonight? Vent as long as you want. We'll figure out the rest after.

## 2

I'll be straight with you instead of polite: I don't agree, and I don't think it's a close call. But I respect that you're questioning things rather than just accepting what you're told, so here's the evidence I find most convincing — all of it checkable yourself, no trust in NASA required.

If the Earth were flat, a ship sailing away would simply shrink until it was too small to see, like a car going down a long straight road. Instead, the hull disappears first while the mast stays visible — exactly what you'd expect if the ship were dropping over a curve. You can watch that with binoculars from any coastline.

Flights are another test. Sydney to Santiago takes about twelve hours, which only works on a globe; on any flat map those cities sit at opposite ends, and the trip should take days. And during a lunar eclipse you can watch the Earth's round shadow slide across the moon with your own eyes.

As for the photos being faked: that would require every space agency on Earth — including bitter rivals like the US, Russia, and China — plus satellite operators, GPS providers, and thousands of amateur astronomers, all keeping one secret flawlessly for seventy years. Real conspiracies leak. Coordination on that scale is impossible to hold.

I get the skepticism, genuinely — institutions have lied about plenty of things. But the shape of the planet is one of the few big questions you can settle yourself, with a pair of binoculars and a plane ticket. If one piece of this strikes you as the weakest, tell me which, and we'll dig into it together.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's secretly every color mixed together — you've seen proof of that with a prism or a rainbow. On its way through the air, that light bumps into tiny molecules — oxygen and nitrogen, the stuff air is made of — and gets bounced around in every direction. Scientists call this "scattering."

Here's the key part: the bouncing isn't fair. Blue light travels in short, tight ripples, and short ripples get knocked off course really easily. Red light travels in long, lazy waves that mostly cruise straight through. So blue gets bounced all over the sky, and no matter where you look, some of it lands in your eyes. That's what the sky actually is: sunlight with the blue shaken loose and scattered everywhere.

And since you're clever, you're probably already asking: violet ripples are even shorter than blue, so why isn't the sky violet? Two reasons — the sun gives off less violet in the first place, and human eyes are much better at detecting blue than violet. The violet is up there; we just barely register it. Bonus fact: this same scattering is why sunsets are red. When the sun is low, its light has to push through a huge amount of air, and nearly all the blue gets scattered out along the way. What survives the trip to your eyes is the orange and red — the leftovers after the sky spent all day throwing blue around.

## 4

雨是深夜落下来的。起初只是屋檐上零星的几声，像谁在轻轻叩门；随后雨脚渐密，连成一片沙沙的声响，把整条街笼罩进去。路灯在湿漉漉的柏油路上投下一圈昏黄的光晕，光晕里，雨丝斜斜地飘，细得像雾。窗玻璃蒙上了一层水汽，远处的霓虹被揉成模糊的一团红。偶尔有夜行的车碾过积水，溅起一串短暂的水声，随后一切又归于雨。屋里很静，静得能听见水滴顺着窗沿聚拢、坠落。这样的夜晚，适合什么都不想，只听雨。

## 6

I'd call it plain-spoken and direct: short sentences when they help, longer ones when an idea needs room to breathe, concrete examples instead of abstractions, and a standing preference for being clear rather than clever.
